title: Vectors
lede: Quantities with both size and direction: forces, velocities, wind. Break them into components, add them, and find the result. How pilots fly through crosswinds and how two tow straps share a load.

sections.md:
## Scalars vs vectors
- **Scalar**: size only. Speed (60 mph), mass, temperature, time.
- **Vector**: size **and** direction. Velocity (60 mph north), force, displacement, acceleration.

A vector is drawn as an arrow: its **length** is its **magnitude**, and it points in its **direction**. Written as **v** (bold) or with an arrow over it.

## Components
Any 2D vector can be split into horizontal and vertical **components**:

**vₓ = |v| cos θ** and **v_y = |v| sin θ** (θ measured from the positive x-axis)

Going back:

**|v| = √(vₓ² + v_y²)** and **θ = tan⁻¹(v_y ÷ vₓ)** (then check the quadrant)

*A force of 100 N at 30°:* Fₓ = 100 cos 30° ≈ 86.6 N, F_y = 100 sin 30° = 50 N.

sections.q: A vector has components (6, 8). Its magnitude is…

sections.md:
## Adding vectors
**Graphically:** place them **tip to tail**; the sum (the **resultant**) runs from the start of the first to the tip of the last.

**With components (the reliable way):** add the x's and add the y's.

(3, 4) + (5, −1) = **(8, 3)**

**Scalar multiplication** stretches a vector: 2(3, 4) = (6, 8), twice as long, same direction. A negative scalar flips it.

sections.title: Two tow straps
sections.problem: Two straps pull a stuck truck: 3,000 N due east and 4,000 N due north. What's the total force?
sections.answer: **5,000 N at about 53° north of east.** Two straps at right angles give less total pull than 7,000 N in a straight line. Angled forces partly work against each other's usefulness.

sections.md:
## Velocity with wind or current
When a plane flies through wind, or a boat crosses a river, its **actual** velocity is the **vector sum** of its own velocity and the wind or current.

*A plane heads due north at 200 km/h with a 50 km/h wind blowing due east.* Ground velocity = (50, 200). Speed = √(2,500 + 40,000) ≈ **206 km/h**, drifting about tan⁻¹(50/200) ≈ **14° east of north**. To actually go north, the pilot must point the nose partly **into** the wind.

Crosswinds push on tall, flat trailers the same way, which is why high-profile vehicles get wind warnings on bridges.

## The dot product
**a · b = aₓbₓ + a_yb_y** = |a||b| cos θ

It measures how much two vectors point the **same way**:
- positive: less than 90° apart
- **zero**: **perpendicular**
- negative: more than 90° apart

In physics, **work = F · d**: only the part of the force along the motion does work. That's the cos θ from the work-and-energy lesson.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Magnitudes don't simply add** unless vectors point the same way. 3 + 4 can be 5.
- **Check the quadrant** after tan⁻¹: (−3, −4) points into quadrant III, not I.
- **Angles from the x-axis** for the cos/sin component formulas. Bearings (from north) need adjusting.
- **Dot product gives a scalar**, not a vector.

practice.q: x-component of a 10 N force at 60°? (cos 60° = 0.5)
If a · b = 0 (both nonzero), the vectors are…
Two perpendicular forces of 6 N and 8 N. Resultant magnitude?
A boat heads straight across a river at 4 m/s; the current flows at 3 m/s downstream. Actual speed?
Direction of the vector (−3, 3), in degrees from the positive x-axis?
practice.why: tan⁻¹(3/−3) gives −45° on a calculator, but the vector points into **quadrant II**: 180° − 45° = **135°**.

practice.q: A 500 N pull at 30° above horizontal drags a sled 10 m along flat ground. Work done? (cos 30° ≈ 0.866)
practice.why: W = F d cos θ = 500 × 10 × 0.866 = **4,330 J**. The upward part of the pull does no work.

practice.q: A plane must reach a city due north, with wind blowing from west to east. The pilot should point the nose…
practice.why: Aim partly **into** the wind so the eastward drift cancels and the resultant points north.
